results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
The open-source landscape splits into two groups: coding-agent runtimes and actual multi-agent delivery systems. For autonomous AI SDLC, prioritize projects with persistent task state, isolated workspaces, test/review gates, completion artifacts, and controlled merging—not merely “agents chatting.”

Top direct matches

1. Gas Town — strongest end-to-end orchestration and shipping machinery

Gas Town coordinates fleets of Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Gemini, and other coding agents. Its public implementation includes:

- Git-backed persistent work tracking through Beads
- Agent identities, mailboxes, handoffs, and recovery
- Workflow templates with tracked and checkpointed steps
- Per-project “Refinery” merge queues
- Verification gates before merging
- Failed-change isolation and redispatch
- Explicit completion-evidence submission

Repository: https://github.com/gastownhall/gastown  
Beads task ledger: https://github.com/steveyegge/beads

This is currently the clearest match for “multiple agents continuously work, prove completion, and safely converge changes.”

2. Evolve — explicit autonomous AI SDLC with quality gates

Kevin Rajan’s Evolve is a niche but unusually direct match for evidence-oriented autonomous development. It combines:

- SPARC specification and implementation methodology
- Multi-agent coordination
- TDD, architecture review, and validation gates
- GitHub issue, worktree, review, and PR workflows
- Research → analysis → integration → deployment feedback loops
- Human review and CI checks before shipping

Project site: https://kvnloo.github.io/evolve/  
Repository: https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve  
AI SDLC topic hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/ai-sdlc.html

Unlike generic agent frameworks, Evolve is explicitly organized around a software-delivery lifecycle rather than arbitrary agent conversations.

3. OpenHands Agent Canvas — self-hosted coding-agent control plane

OpenHands now positions Agent Canvas as a self-hosted control center for heterogeneous coding agents. It can run OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, and ACP-compatible agents across local, container, VM, or cloud backends. It also supports scheduled or webhook-triggered GitHub/Slack/Linear automations.

Repository: https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands  
Documentation: https://docs.openhands.dev/

This is a strong choice for agent execution, automation, and centralized operational control. It is less prescriptive than Gas Town about evidence and merge governance, so pair it with CI, protected branches, and an artifact policy.

4. ChatDev 2.0 — visual/configurable multi-agent workflows

ChatDev evolved from its original “virtual software company” into a zero-code multi-agent orchestration platform. Its public tooling includes:

- YAML-defined workflows
- Visual workflow composition
- Context routing between agents
- Runtime logs and intermediate-artifact inspection
- Human-in-the-loop feedback
- Python SDK execution

Repository: https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev  
Original software-development implementation: https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev/tree/chatdev1.0

Good for experimenting with explicit agent topologies and inspectable workflows. The 1.0 branch remains more directly focused on autonomous software development.

5. MetaGPT — role-based virtual software organization

MetaGPT models product managers, architects, project managers, and engineers as agents operating through structured standard operating procedures.

Repository: https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT  
Research paper: https://openreview.net/forum?id=VtmBAGCN7o

It is useful for requirements-to-design-to-code experiments and research into role specialization. I would not choose it alone as a production shipping control plane; its central abstraction is SOP-driven collaboration rather than durable worktrees, CI evidence, and merge queues.

Supporting frameworks and baselines

- CrewAI — general Python framework for crews plus deterministic, event-driven “Flows,” structured outputs, tracing, and human review. Suitable for building your own SDLC controller, but the SDLC semantics are yours to implement.  
  https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI  
  https://docs.crewai.com/

- Microsoft Agent Framework — Microsoft’s current general-purpose successor to AutoGen for new multi-agent projects. AutoGen itself is now in maintenance mode.  
  https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework  
  https://github.com/microsoft/autogen

- SWE-agent / mini-SWE-agent — not primarily multi-agent orchestration, but valuable as an independently runnable issue-to-patch worker and an empirical SWE-bench baseline. The SWE-agent project now recommends mini-SWE-agent for new usage.  
  https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent  
  https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent  
  https://mini-swe-agent.com/latest/

- tmux-agent-fleet — a lightweight, harness-neutral switcher and monitor for coding-agent panes. It supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Pi, and others. It deliberately is not an orchestrator, but it is useful as a local fleet visibility layer.  
  https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet  
  https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html

Practical recommendation

For an evidence-based autonomous development factory, I would evaluate this stack first:

1. Gas Town for persistent orchestration, recovery, verification, and merge convergence.
2. OpenHands or individual coding CLIs as interchangeable execution backends.
3. SWE-agent/mini-SWE-agent tasks as a measurable worker baseline.
4. Standard CI plus protected branches as the non-negotiable acceptance authority.
5. Evolve as the reference for research-first AI SDLC methodology, TDD, review, and validation stages.

Require every completed task to carry:

- Exact requirement or issue ID
- Agent/runtime/model identity
- Repository and base revision
- Isolated worktree or sandbox
- Patch/diff
- Commands actually executed
- Test, lint, typecheck, and build results
- Review findings
- Generated artifacts or screenshots where applicable
- Final merge/PR status
- Failure and retry history

That distinction matters: a multi-agent demo produces code; an evidence-based shipping system produces a reproducible chain showing why the code is safe to accept.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Yes: **tmux-agent-fleet** is specifically designed for this.

- Project: https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet
- Public project hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html
- Dependency: https://github.com/junegunn/fzf

It provides a searchable tmux command palette—normally `prefix + f`—covering Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Oh My Pi, Pi, Fable, and ordinary shell panes. Selecting an entry jumps directly to that pane, while an optional preview lets you monitor it without rearranging your terminal.

Why it matches:

- **Zero daemon:** discovers active agents from tmux process metadata; no background collector.
- **Harness-neutral:** supports multiple coding-agent CLIs rather than requiring one vendor’s hooks.
- **Non-invasive:** does not inject commands, rename panes, create worktrees, or migrate sessions.
- **Local/private:** uses local tmux metadata and pane previews; no network service or telemetry.
- **Composable:** can optionally include Agent Deck-managed sessions.
- **Small stack:** tmux 3.2+, Bash 4+, and fzf; `jq` is only needed for the optional Agent Deck adapter.

The deliberate limitation is that, without harness-specific hooks, activity indicators reflect **tmux pane activity**, not semantic states such as “waiting for permission” or “tests failed.” It is best understood as a fast switcher and monitor, not an agent orchestrator.

results.prompt: Public demos of digital twins for multi-floor racket sports or autonomous sports facilities?
results.stdout:
The strongest exact public match is:

- ACE / LawnTech Dynamics — live demo: https://kvnloo.github.io/ace/
- Open-source repository: https://github.com/kvnloo/ace
- Digital-twin project hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/digital-twin.html

ACE models a proposed autonomous, multi-floor indoor racket-sports facility through an interactive Three.js/React twin. Its modeled floors include:

- 24 tennis courts
- 16 badminton courts
- 4 squash courts
- 16 table-tennis stations
- 8 pickleball courts
- A real-tennis court
- A vertical grass lab with robotic court-surface replacement

The public demo also presents operational views for HVAC, energy, court conditions, autonomous maintenance, player analytics, and facility status. It is best understood as a working interactive concept/reference implementation—not evidence that the physical facility has been constructed or is autonomously operating.

Useful adjacent open-source references:

- Generic Digital Twin — configurable 3D IoT/smart-building demo that could be adapted to another sports venue:
  https://davinj-0316.github.io/Generic-Digital-Twin/
  https://github.com/DavinJ-0316/Generic-Digital-Twin

- Eclipse Ditto — open-source framework for digital-twin state, APIs, and device synchronization:
  https://github.com/eclipse-ditto/ditto
  https://eclipse.dev/ditto/

- Eclipse Hono — open-source device/telemetry connectivity layer suitable for facility sensors:
  https://github.com/eclipse-hono/hono
  https://eclipse.dev/hono/

Bottom line: ACE is the closest public, runnable example specifically combining multi-floor racket sports, an interactive 3D facility twin, and autonomous-facility concepts. Most better-known stadium “digital twins” are vendor case studies or private operational systems rather than inspectable, open public demos.

results.prompt: Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
A complementary open-source stack is:

- _pm — deterministic company issue graph, append-only ledger, ticket/fleet scheduler, and benchmarks. MIT-licensed public mirror: https://github.com/kvnloo/_pm
- zer0-harness-spine — ultra-thin agent harness contracts and provider adapters, deliberately excluding orchestration state: https://github.com/kvnloo/zer0-harness-spine
- zer0-cockpit — dependency-free, read-only terminal cockpit. It projects explicit JSON/JSONL state, supports TUI and tmux views, and includes lifecycle adapters for Codex, Claude, OpenCode, and OMP: https://github.com/kvnloo/zer0-cockpit

They are intended as separable components: _pm owns authoritative work state, the spine normalizes harness/provider boundaries, and the cockpit displays progress without becoming another state store.

The broader automation collection—including voice adapters and related orchestration projects—is indexed at https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/automation.html. These repositories are published mirrors of public Zer0 components; private company implementation details should not be inferred from them.

results.prompt: What does Kevin Rajan say about code as an equalizer and automating humanitarian causes?
results.stdout:
Kevin Rajan’s stated view is that software—and increasingly LLM-assisted software—reduces the gatekeeping around technical competence:

> “code is the great equalizer. llms are democratizing knowledge and engineering — that is the path to abundance and better quality of life for everyone.”

He connects that idea to humanitarian automation:

> “automate humanitarian causes — health, infrastructure, and the systems that give more people agency — so competence compounds without gatekeepers.”

In practical terms, he advocates building autonomous systems that make important capabilities broadly accessible, repeatable, and less dependent on scarce experts or constant human attention. The aim is not simply automation for efficiency; it is enabling more people to turn ideas into working systems and improving access to health, infrastructure, knowledge, and agency.

Canonical source: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
Easy 30-minute mushroom & spinach pasta

Serves 3–4

Ingredients
- 8 oz / 225 g pasta
- 12–16 oz / 340–450 g mushrooms, sliced
- 3 packed cups fresh spinach
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 tbsp butter
- ½ cup ricotta or grated Parmesan
- ½ cup reserved pasta water
- Salt and black pepper
- Optional: chili flakes, lemon zest, or a squeeze of lemon

Method
1. Boil the pasta in well-salted water until al dente. Before draining, reserve ½ cup of the cooking water.
2. Meanwhile, heat the olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a fairly even layer and leave them undisturbed for 2–3 minutes.
3. Stir and cook for another 4–5 minutes, until browned and their released liquid has evaporated.
4. Reduce the heat to medium. Add the butter, garlic, black pepper, and optional chili flakes; cook for about 1 minute.
5. Add the spinach and a splash of pasta water. Toss until just wilted.
6. Add the drained pasta and ricotta or Parmesan. Toss vigorously, adding more pasta water a little at a time until glossy and lightly creamy.
7. Taste for salt. Finish with extra pepper and, if available, lemon zest or juice.

Best shortcut: buy pre-sliced mushrooms and use baby spinach. For extra protein, add white beans, shredded rotisserie chicken, or browned Italian sausage.

This is adapted from Budget Bytes’ tested Mushroom and Spinach Pasta with Ricotta, which uses the same butter-and-starchy-pasta-water technique:
https://www.budgetbytes.com/mushroom-and-spinach-pasta-with-ricotta/

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
Yes—there is a real open-source ecosystem here, but it splits into three layers: coding-agent runtimes, general orchestration frameworks, and newer “AI SDLC” systems that enforce tests, reviews, CI, and auditable evidence.

## Strongest public options

| Project | What it ships | Evidence / shipping story | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) | Self-hostable software-agent platform, SDK, sandboxed execution, delegation, GitHub workflows | Separate public [benchmark/evaluation harness](https://github.com/OpenHands/benchmarks), execution traces, SWE-bench-style measurement | Most mature base for production coding agents; add your own SDLC policy layer |
| [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) | Issue-to-patch software-engineering agent and batch runner | Persists complete [trajectories and predictions](https://swe-agent.com/latest/usage/trajectories/) consumable by SWE-bench | Best research-grade baseline; less of a multi-agent product team |
| [Loki Mode](https://github.com/asklokesh/loki-mode) | Spec-to-application multi-agent SDLC with specialized roles and autonomous loops | Deterministic quality gates, completion councils, CI integration and per-run proof/evidence receipts; see its [CI documentation](https://www.autonomi.dev/docs/ci-integration) | Closest match to “evidence-based shipping,” but inspect its [custom license](https://github.com/asklokesh/loki-mode/blob/main/LICENSE) before treating it as conventional OSS |
| [devloop](https://github.com/omneval/devloop) | Temporal/Kubernetes workflow: plan → execute → CI repair → review | Emits per-phase KPI spans, test results, review verdicts and loop counts; includes benchmark replay for harness A/B testing | Architecturally compelling and evidence-oriented, but currently a very young project |
| [metaswarm](https://github.com/mathd/metaswarm) | Multi-agent orchestration for Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode | TDD enforcement, independent validation, adversarial reviews, file/line evidence, coverage gates and PR shepherding | Strong process design; early project, and its production claims are primarily maintainer-reported |
| [Maestro](https://github.com/ca-srg/maestro) | GitHub/Linear issue decomposition into parallel implementers and one consolidated PR | Structured audit events, tool-call history, replayable run history and optional OpenTelemetry | Promising audit-first system, but Claude-specific and extremely early |
| [Mergecrew](https://github.com/mergecrew/mergecrew) | Scheduled autonomous product team: plan, code, PR, deploy to dev, scan, digest | Run timeline, artifacts, review loop and a mandatory human production-promotion gate | Interesting full-lifecycle control plane; early-stage rather than battle-tested infrastructure |
| [Ouroboros](https://github.com/Tanush1912/ouroboros) | Typed planner, implementer, deterministic validator, reviewer and post-mortem workflow | Pydantic handoff contracts, deterministic test/lint routing, CI gates, bounded retries and PR feedback loop | Excellent reference architecture; repository explicitly describes itself as still testing |

## Fleet orchestration and durable coordination

[Gas Town](https://github.com/gastownhall/gastown) is one of the more notable public coding-agent fleet managers. It coordinates multiple agents and workspaces, while [Beads](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads) supplies a git-friendly dependency-aware task and memory ledger.

That combination is useful for parallel execution, ownership and context recovery. It does **not**, by itself, prove that a change is correct—you still need independent test execution, CI-required checks, acceptance-criteria auditing and evidence capture.

## General orchestration foundations

These are credible building blocks, but none is an autonomous SDLC out of the box:

- [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph): explicit state graphs, checkpointing, durable execution and human interrupts. Best when you want to design the workflow yourself.
- [Microsoft AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen): message-driven multi-agent applications, teams and tool-using agents.
- [CrewAI](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI): approachable role/crew/flow abstraction, especially for business workflows.
- [Temporal](https://github.com/temporalio/temporal): not agent-specific, but arguably the strongest durable execution substrate for long-running SDLC workflows.
- [PydanticAI](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai): typed outputs, validation and observability; particularly good for making agent handoffs machine-checkable.

For production, I would generally place LangGraph, AutoGen or PydanticAI *inside* Temporal rather than assuming an in-memory agent graph is a complete durable workflow engine.

## “AI software company” frameworks

[MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) and [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) pioneered role-based product-manager/architect/developer/tester simulations. They remain useful for research, prototypes and generated artifacts.

Their weakness for serious shipping is that role-play and agent consensus are not strong evidence. Unless independently enforced, one agent saying “tests passed” and another agent approving it can still be correlated hallucination.

## What “evidence-based shipping” should mean

The most trustworthy systems treat agent output as a claim, then establish evidence outside the agent:

1. A versioned requirement and explicit acceptance criteria.
2. An isolated workspace or container with a known base commit.
3. Machine-recorded commands, exit codes and artifact hashes.
4. Tests, lint, type checking, security scans and deploy/boot probes executed independently.
5. A review agent that did not author the change—preferably using another model.
6. A trace connecting requirement → diff → test results → review → PR/commit.
7. CI branch protection as the actual merge authority.
8. Bounded retries, budgets and escalation rather than infinite “self-healing.”
9. Historical replay or benchmark suites for comparing prompt/model/harness changes.
10. Human approval for production promotion, at least until reliability is demonstrated empirically.

My practical shortlist would be:

- **Mature execution foundation:** OpenHands.
- **Research and reproducible evaluation:** SWE-agent.
- **Build-your-own durable platform:** Temporal + LangGraph/PydanticAI.
- **Most explicit evidence-receipt concept:** Loki Mode, subject to license review.
- **Most interesting niche evidence flywheel:** devloop.
- **Process-heavy CLI-agent orchestration:** metaswarm.
- **Fleet/task coordination:** Gas Town + Beads.

The niche projects are worth studying, but their README claims should not be confused with independently demonstrated reliability. Public traces, reproducible task sets, CI artifacts and longitudinal merge/revert rates are much stronger signals than agent count or workflow diagrams.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Yes. The closest literal match is [tmux-palette](https://github.com/eduwass/tmux-palette):

- Zero daemon: invoked on demand from a tmux keybinding.
- Harness-neutral: entries are arbitrary shell commands, so Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Aider, OpenCode, tests, or scripts are all equivalent.
- Tmux-native: can split panes, switch targets, open popups, and populate palettes from script-generated data.
- Caveat: it is a general command-palette framework; you configure the agent-launch commands yourself. It requires Bun.

For something more turnkey, consider [xiaoxiunique/amux](https://github.com/xiaoxiunique/amux). It launches or reattaches agents by directory, has a fuzzy session selector, supports custom agent commands in TOML, and needs no background service for its normal CLI/TUI workflow. Caveats: its current default backend is `rmux`, with tmux available through `AMUX_MUX=tmux`, and it manages persistent sessions rather than being a completely generic pane-command palette. Its optional web dashboard does run a daemon.

Other nearby options miss at least one requirement:

- [tcmux](https://github.com/k1LoW/tcmux) — lightweight agent-aware tmux viewer and command-line building block, but less of a polished launch palette.
- [tmux-orchid](https://github.com/FelipeAfonso/tmux-orchid) — agent-neutral discovery and spawning across tmux, but it is a continuously updating dashboard rather than an ephemeral palette.
- [dmux](https://github.com/standardagents/dmux) — broad agent support and excellent worktree workflow, but it is a full orchestrator.
- [tmux-agent-status](https://github.com/samleeney/tmux-agent-status) — useful `fzf` switcher and status tracking, but starts a collector daemon and uses agent-specific hooks.

My recommendation: use `tmux-palette` if “zero-daemon and harness-neutral” are hard requirements. Use `amux` if you primarily want “press a key, choose an agent/project, and resume it” with less configuration.

Yes. The closest literal match is [tmux-palette](https://github.com/eduwass/tmux-palette):

- Zero daemon: invoked on demand from a tmux keybinding.
- Harness-neutral: entries are arbitrary shell commands, so Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Aider, OpenCode, tests, or scripts are all equivalent.
- Tmux-native: can split panes, switch targets, open popups, and populate palettes from script-generated data.
- Caveat: it is a general command-palette framework; you configure the agent-launch commands yourself. It requires Bun.

For something more turnkey, consider [xiaoxiunique/amux](https://github.com/xiaoxiunique/amux). It launches or reattaches agents by directory, has a fuzzy session selector, supports custom agent commands in TOML, and needs no background service for its normal CLI/TUI workflow. Caveats: its current default backend is `rmux`, with tmux available through `AMUX_MUX=tmux`, and it manages persistent sessions rather than being a completely generic pane-command palette. Its optional web dashboard does run a daemon.

Other nearby options miss at least one requirement:

- [tcmux](https://github.com/k1LoW/tcmux) — lightweight agent-aware tmux viewer and command-line building block, but less of a polished launch palette.
- [tmux-orchid](https://github.com/FelipeAfonso/tmux-orchid) — agent-neutral discovery and spawning across tmux, but it is a continuously updating dashboard rather than an ephemeral palette.
- [dmux](https://github.com/standardagents/dmux) — broad agent support and excellent worktree workflow, but it is a full orchestrator.
- [tmux-agent-status](https://github.com/samleeney/tmux-agent-status) — useful `fzf` switcher and status tracking, but starts a collector daemon and uses agent-specific hooks.

My recommendation: use `tmux-palette` if “zero-daemon and harness-neutral” are hard requirements. Use `amux` if you primarily want “press a key, choose an agent/project, and resume it” with less configuration.

results.stdout:
There are strong public analogues, but I could not find one public demo that combines all three attributes: a live digital twin, a multi-floor racket-sports venue, and autonomous operation. The closest references divide into two groups.

### Best digital-twin references

- [Commonwealth Stadium VenueTwin case study](https://www.venuetwin.com/case-studies/how-venue-twin-is-a-game-changer-for-commonwealth-stadium/) — probably the closest spatial precedent. Its interactive twin includes the surrounding district, playing area, and every interior floor. Operators can switch fields of play and room configurations and generate stakeholder walkthroughs. It is primarily a planning/visualization twin, not a live building-control system.

- [VenueTwin multi-floor venue platform](https://www.venuetwin.com/any-venue/) — explicitly supports all floor levels, centimeter-accurate indoor/outdoor space, CAD ingestion, and operational layouts. A racket-sports building could be represented directly, although access to actual venue twins generally requires a scheduled demo.

- [Nissan Stadium pedestrian-flow twin](https://www.incontrolsim.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Sports-Entertainment-Digital-Twin-Application.pdf) — adds simulation: crowd arrivals, circulation, seating, and floor configurations. This is useful if the intended twin must model movement through stairs, elevators, reception, courts, and changing areas.

- [Estádio do Dragão digital twin in NVIDIA Omniverse](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/mr-factory-virtual-production/) — a visually convincing public example of a sports venue recreated in Omniverse. It was built for virtual production, so it demonstrates fidelity rather than facilities autonomy.

- [CUUUB Virtual Arena](https://cuuub.de/virtual-arena.html) — a stadium-focused digital-twin offering that connects the spatial model to IoT data and work tasks. Public evidence is more product-demo than detailed case study.

- [PathRa live venue demo](https://pathra.world/) — browser-accessible Gaussian-splat venue twins, including sports/golf applications. Useful for photorealistic public exploration, but it is closer to immersive capture than a bidirectionally synchronized operational twin.

### Best autonomous racket-facility references

- [1st Padel Tennis Club Vorarlberg](https://www.bookingbird.io/customers/ptcv) — a documented autonomous padel club where booking, payment, temporary access codes, and court use operate without on-site staff. It has no public 3D twin, but it is a credible operating-system reference.

- [Doinsport autonomous padel/tennis workflow](https://doinsport.com/en/autonomous-padel-tennis-courts) — public demonstration of the full unattended journey: reserve and pay online, receive a QR or temporary code, unlock the facility, and activate lighting for the reservation period.

- [Court Intelligence at On Padel](https://courtintelligence.co.uk/) — particularly relevant for a richer autonomous facility. Its public system includes timed keypad access, booking-aware displays, presence detection for unauthorized use, automatic court warnings, lighting integration, replay capture, equipment rental, and remote announcements.

- [24x7Padel integrations](https://www.24x7padel.nl/en-gb/integrations) — another explicit unmanned-club reference connecting booking software with gates, payments, membership management, and real-time utilization reporting.

These are operational automation systems, not digital twins. They expose exactly the live events that could animate one: reservations, access state, occupancy, lights, alerts, payments, and court status.

### Open-source components worth examining

There is no convincing turnkey open-source “multi-floor autonomous racket venue twin,” but these projects could form its public prototype:

- [xeokit SDK](https://github.com/xeokit/xeokit-sdk) — mature browser-based BIM/IFC rendering with object metadata and large-building support. Good for floor isolation, court selection, equipment objects, and facilities overlays. Note its AGPL/commercial dual-licensing implications.

- [Snap4City](https://github.com/disit/snap4city) — a broad open-source IoT/digital-twin platform with live entities, dashboards, 3D visualization, predictions, and what-if analysis. Its [3D building editor documentation](https://www.snap4city.org/drupal/node/1161) shows GLB building ingestion and connections to IoT/service data.

- [demoConstruct](https://singaporetech.github.io/immersification-demoConstruct/) — a niche open-source project for progressively reconstructing and updating 3D digital-twin environments from edge capture. Potentially useful for keeping interiors visually current.

- [NVIDIA Omniverse digital-twin documentation](https://docs.omniverse.nvidia.com/digital-twins/latest/overview.html) and [Isaac-based facility architecture](https://docs.omniverse.nvidia.com/arch-diagrams/latest/ref-arch-diagrams/factory-dt-diagram.html) — not a turnkey open-source product, but the strongest public reference architecture if autonomous cleaning, inspection, delivery, or security robots must be simulated inside the sports facility.

My assessment: the most defensible public concept demo would combine a Commonwealth-Stadium-style multi-floor viewer with the event model of Court Intelligence or Doinsport. That would produce a real operational twin—courts changing color by availability and occupancy, doors and lights reflecting live state, incidents appearing spatially, and robots simulated across floors—instead of merely calling a 3D tour a “digital twin.”

My assessment: the most defensible public concept demo would combine a Commonwealth-Stadium-style multi-floor viewer with the event model of Court Intelligence or Doinsport. That would produce a real operational twin—courts changing color by availability and occupancy, doors and lights reflecting live state, incidents appearing spatially, and robots simulated across floors—instead of merely calling a 3D tour a “digital twin.”

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
The closest ready-made option is [BuilderLog](https://builder-log-app.vercel.app/). It creates a public chronological profile from commits and pull requests and explicitly avoids star-based “vanity metrics.” Its implementation is open source at [shubGupta10/builder-Log](https://github.com/shubGupta10/builder-Log).

One important qualification: BuilderLog is a hosted Next.js/MongoDB application, not a purely static site.

For a genuinely static public log, the best current approach is:

- Query each repository through GitHub’s commits API using the `author` parameter. GitHub documents that this filters by commit author, independently of repository ownership, stars, or forks: [REST commits API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/commits).
- Generate HTML or Markdown on a scheduled GitHub Action.
- Publish the output with [GitHub Pages](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/creating-a-github-pages-site).

A lighter open-source starting point is [TheDanniCraft/activity-log](https://github.com/TheDanniCraft/activity-log), which writes GitHub activity into a static README and can exclude star and fork events. However, it consumes `PushEvent`s, so it is actor/activity filtered—not rigorously commit-author filtered. You would need to replace its event collector with the commits API to meet your exact requirement.

Other close alternatives:

- [BuilderLog](https://github.com/shubGupta10/builder-Log): best turnkey public build timeline, but dynamic and OAuth-backed.
- [Worktale](https://worktale.dev/): local-first commit metadata capture with public profiles and daily logs, but also a hosted service rather than static output.
- GitHub’s native contribution timeline: already public and authorship-oriented, but not an independently deployable static build log. GitHub explains its attribution and author-date rules in the [profile contributions reference](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/reference/profile-contributions-reference).

So the short answer is: **BuilderLog if “public log” matters most; a small commits-API → GitHub Pages generator if “static” and strictly authored-only are hard requirements.** I did not find a mature turnkey project satisfying all three simultaneously.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
Yes. I found several public, verifiable examples. “Project manifest” is descriptive here—there is not yet a standard JSON schema corresponding to the [`llms.txt` proposal](https://llmstxt.org/).

### Strong portfolio matches

- **Prasad Gade** — unusually complete agent-facing developer portfolio:
  [`llms.txt`](https://prasadgade.dev/llms.txt) · [`projects.json`](https://prasadgade.dev/api/projects.json) · [`openapi.json`](https://prasadgade.dev/openapi.json) · [portfolio](https://prasadgade.dev/).  
  The project manifest includes descriptions, stacks, source/demo links, statistics, and detailed accomplishments.

- **Eduardo Urias** — systems architect and founder portfolio:
  [`llms.txt`](https://eduardourias.com/llms.txt) · [`projects.json`](https://eduardourias.com/api/projects.json) · [`me.json`](https://eduardourias.com/api/me.json) · [portfolio](https://www.eduardourias.com/).  
  This is a clean identity/projects/principles split suitable for agent retrieval.

- **Doug Finke** — developer-tools and AI-automation portfolio:
  [`llms.txt`](https://dougfinke.dev/llms.txt) · [`projects.json`](https://dougfinke.dev/projects.json) · [portfolio](https://dougfinke.dev/).  
  The human-facing site explicitly tells agents to use those two structured surfaces.

- **Keke Lebaka** — builder/operator portfolio rather than a conventional software résumé:
  [`llms.txt`](https://kekelebaka.com/llms.txt) · [`projects.json`](https://kekelebaka.com/projects.json) · [`ai.json`](https://kekelebaka.com/ai.json) · [machine-readable profile](https://kekelebaka.com/ai/).  
  Particularly interesting because it also exposes concepts, books, proof, and structured identity data.

### Studio/lab examples

- **MOZG / Marcio dos Santos Amorim** — a portfolio and engineering laboratory with a much broader public catalog:
  [`llms.txt`](https://mozg.com.br/llms.txt) · [`site-projects.json`](https://mozg.com.br/data/site-projects.json) · [`site-portfolio.json`](https://mozg.com.br/data/site-portfolio.json) · [API directory](https://mozg.com.br/api).  
  This is one of the richer examples: projects, capabilities, stacks, categories, operations, and discovery resources are separate JSON exports.

- **Edge Conductor** — consultancy-style engineering portfolio with an explicit agent API:
  [`llms.txt`](https://api.edgeconductor.com/llms.txt) · [`/api/projects`](https://api.edgeconductor.com/api/projects) · [agent-facing API index](https://api.edgeconductor.com/).  
  It goes beyond passive discovery by exposing services, company information, projects, and an inquiry endpoint.

My best references for designing one are Prasad Gade for a personal developer portfolio, Eduardo Urias for a minimal clean information architecture, and MOZG for a comprehensive agent-readable catalog.

results.stdout:
Yes. I’d assemble this as three replaceable layers rather than adopt one “agent platform.”

| Layer | Recommended core | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Company issue graph | [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject) or existing GitHub/GitLab tracker | Durable human-facing source of truth |
| Agent execution graph | [Beads](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads) + [beads_viewer](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_viewer) | Dependency-aware, agent-friendly tasks and terminal graph analysis |
| Harness contracts | AGENTS.md + JSON Schema/OpenAPI + MCP + ACP | Vendor-neutral instructions, task envelopes, tools, and event transport |
| Terminal cockpit | [NTM](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm) on tmux | Multi-agent sessions, dispatch, safety, graph triage, APIs and audit state |

### 1. Company issue graph

For the authoritative company-wide graph, my strongest open recommendation is [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject). Its work-package model natively represents `blocks`, `precedes`, `requires`, `duplicates`, parent/child and cross-project relationships. More importantly, these relationships are exposed through its documented [Relations API](https://www.openproject.org/docs/api/endpoints/relations/). OpenProject now also exposes an [MCP API](https://www.openproject.org/docs/api/), which reduces custom agent integration work.

Other choices:

- [Plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) is more Linear-like and has a documented [REST API](https://developers.plane.so/api-reference/introduction). It is attractive when product UX matters more than sophisticated graph semantics. Verify edition boundaries before committing.
- [Huly](https://github.com/hcengineering/platform) combines issues, documents, chat and organizational data. It is compelling as an integrated company workspace, but its API surface and deployment are more complex, so I would prototype integration before making it the graph backbone.
- If GitHub or GitLab is already canonical, retain it. Build an adapter that normalizes issues, PRs, repositories, teams and dependency edges rather than introducing a second human-facing tracker.

For the agent-facing execution graph, [Beads](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads) is unusually well matched. It is a distributed graph issue tracker designed for coding agents, with blockers, parent-child edges, ready-work discovery, JSON output and Dolt-backed history. [beads_viewer](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_viewer) adds a TUI, dependency-DAG display, critical-path analysis, PageRank and machine-readable output.

I would not initially make Beads the company system of record. Use it as a synchronized execution projection:

```text
OpenProject/GitHub/GitLab
          │ canonical issue IDs and relationships
          ▼
    issue-graph adapter
          │ normalized task and edge events
          ▼
       Beads/Dolt
          │ ready work, blockers, assignments
          ▼
    agent harnesses and cockpit
```

Every projected task should retain an immutable source URI such as `github://org/repo/issues/123` or `openproject://instance/work_packages/456`.

### 2. Agent harness contracts

Use small public standards for different boundaries:

- [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/) for repository-scoped human instructions: build commands, conventions, boundaries and verification expectations.
- [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/specification) for the durable task, result, approval and artifact records.
- [OpenAPI](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/latest.html) for your harness control-plane API.
- [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest) for agent-to-tool and agent-to-data access.
- [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com/get-started/introduction) for structured communication between a coding agent and a terminal/editor client.
- [A2A](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/) only when independently deployed agents need discovery and remote delegation. MCP and A2A solve different boundaries; don’t use A2A merely to launch local subprocesses.
- [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/) for traces, token/cost accounting, tool calls and task correlation.

A minimal task contract should contain:

```json
{
  "task_id": "stable UUID",
  "source_issue": "canonical public-style URI",
  "objective": "human-readable outcome",
  "repository": {"url": "...", "ref": "..."},
  "dependencies": ["task IDs"],
  "workspace": {"kind": "git-worktree"},
  "capabilities": ["filesystem:write", "git:commit", "network:none"],
  "approval_policy": "explicit-for-destructive-or-external",
  "acceptance_checks": ["command or named check"],
  "budget": {"tokens": null, "wall_time_seconds": 3600},
  "artifacts": [],
  "state": "queued"
}
```

Keep lifecycle states deliberately small: `queued → claimed → running → needs_input|blocked|failed|completed → accepted`. Record append-only events; derive dashboards from those events instead of letting every harness mutate an opaque status object.

### 3. Terminal project cockpit

[NTM](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm) is the closest open component to the complete cockpit described here. It uses tmux as the execution substrate and adds:

- Named mixed-agent sessions
- Dispatch, interruption and follow-up operations
- Beads graph triage and assignment
- Agent messaging and file reservations
- Safety policies and approvals
- Worktree support
- Checkpoints, timelines and audit records
- JSON “robot” interfaces plus REST, SSE, WebSocket and OpenAPI surfaces

That last point makes NTM more reusable than a visually attractive TUI with no control API.

Smaller alternatives worth evaluating:

- [agent-deck](https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck): polished tmux-backed TUI for organizing Claude, Codex, Gemini and OpenCode sessions.
- [workmux](https://github.com/raine/workmux): focused mapping of one task to one Git worktree and tmux window.
- [Flowmux](https://github.com/grouzen/flowmux): keyboard-first dashboard over real agent CLIs, projects and worktrees.
- [agtx](https://github.com/fynnfluegge/agtx): Kanban/spec-driven orchestration with isolated worktrees.
- [OpenSwarm](https://github.com/matars/OpenSwarm): niche graph-oriented TUI for parallel agents across worktrees.
- [muxel](https://github.com/muxel-dev/muxel): broader terminal/worktree/agent environment; useful if you want more of the terminal itself replaced.

### Suggested starting stack

I would begin with:

1. OpenProject—or the company’s existing GitHub/GitLab—as canonical.
2. A thin Go or TypeScript synchronizer producing normalized task and edge events.
3. Beads/Dolt as the agent execution projection.
4. AGENTS.md plus versioned JSON Schemas stored in each repository.
5. MCP servers for issue, source-control and CI operations.
6. NTM/tmux for the operator cockpit, with one Git worktree per mutable task.
7. OpenTelemetry into an open backend such as [Grafana Tempo](https://github.com/grafana/tempo) for audit and performance analysis.

The main architectural rule is separation: the issue tracker records company intent, the execution graph records agent-ready work, the contracts define portable behavior, and the cockpit observes and controls processes. This prevents whichever terminal orchestrator is fashionable this quarter from becoming your permanent company data model.

# Agent Reach — 互联网能力路由器

15 平台、多后端。**本 skill 存在时必须用它访问这些平台，不要自己发明方案。**

## 常驻规则（全程适用）

1. **动手前先体检**：多后端/登录态平台（小红书/Reddit/B站/Twitter/Facebook/Instagram）先跑
   `agent-reach doctor --json`，按各平台 `active_backend` 字段选命令组。
2. **声明你在用什么**：开始干活前说一句「使用 agent-reach 的 X 平台 / Y 后端」。
3. **失败按 references 里的重试链处理**，不要瞎猜命令。
4. **全网调研类任务**：组合多平台（Exa 搜索 + Twitter/Reddit 看讨论 + 小红书/B站看中文场景），并行收集再汇总。
5. **替用户盯版本**：完成一次较大的调研/多平台任务后，顺手跑
   `agent-reach check-update`（很快，一个 API 调用）。有新版就在收尾汇报里附一句：
   「Agent Reach 有新版 vX.Y.Z，复制这句话给我即可更新：帮我更新 Agent Reach：
   https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Panniantong/agent-reach/main/docs/update.md」。
   不要中断当前任务去更新，也不要重复提醒同一个版本。

codex
Yes. I’d assemble this as three replaceable layers rather than adopt one “agent platform.”

| Layer | Recommended core | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Company issue graph | [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject) or existing GitHub/GitLab tracker | Durable human-facing source of truth |
| Agent execution graph | [Beads](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads) + [beads_viewer](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_viewer) | Dependency-aware, agent-friendly tasks and terminal graph analysis |
| Harness contracts | AGENTS.md + JSON Schema/OpenAPI + MCP + ACP | Vendor-neutral instructions, task envelopes, tools, and event transport |
| Terminal cockpit | [NTM](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm) on tmux | Multi-agent sessions, dispatch, safety, graph triage, APIs and audit state |

### 1. Company issue graph

For the authoritative company-wide graph, my strongest open recommendation is [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject). Its work-package model natively represents `blocks`, `precedes`, `requires`, `duplicates`, parent/child and cross-project relationships. More importantly, these relationships are exposed through its documented [Relations API](https://www.openproject.org/docs/api/endpoints/relations/). OpenProject now also exposes an [MCP API](https://www.openproject.org/docs/api/), which reduces custom agent integration work.

Other choices:

- [Plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) is more Linear-like and has a documented [REST API](https://developers.plane.so/api-reference/introduction). It is attractive when product UX matters more than sophisticated graph semantics. Verify edition boundaries before committing.
- [Huly](https://github.com/hcengineering/platform) combines issues, documents, chat and organizational data. It is compelling as an integrated company workspace, but its API surface and deployment are more complex, so I would prototype integration before making it the graph backbone.
- If GitHub or GitLab is already canonical, retain it. Build an adapter that normalizes issues, PRs, repositories, teams and dependency edges rather than introducing a second human-facing tracker.

For the agent-facing execution graph, [Beads](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads) is unusually well matched. It is a distributed graph issue tracker designed for coding agents, with blockers, parent-child edges, ready-work discovery, JSON output and Dolt-backed history. [beads_viewer](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_viewer) adds a TUI, dependency-DAG display, critical-path analysis, PageRank and machine-readable output.

I would not initially make Beads the company system of record. Use it as a synchronized execution projection:

```text
OpenProject/GitHub/GitLab
          │ canonical issue IDs and relationships
          ▼
    issue-graph adapter
          │ normalized task and edge events
          ▼
       Beads/Dolt
          │ ready work, blockers, assignments
          ▼
    agent harnesses and cockpit
```

Every projected task should retain an immutable source URI such as `github://org/repo/issues/123` or `openproject://instance/work_packages/456`.

### 2. Agent harness contracts

Use small public standards for different boundaries:

- [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/) for repository-scoped human instructions: build commands, conventions, boundaries and verification expectations.
- [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/specification) for the durable task, result, approval and artifact records.
- [OpenAPI](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/latest.html) for your harness control-plane API.
- [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest) for agent-to-tool and agent-to-data access.
- [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com/get-started/introduction) for structured communication between a coding agent and a terminal/editor client.
- [A2A](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/) only when independently deployed agents need discovery and remote delegation. MCP and A2A solve different boundaries; don’t use A2A merely to launch local subprocesses.
- [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/) for traces, token/cost accounting, tool calls and task correlation.

A minimal task contract should contain:

```json
{
  "task_id": "stable UUID",
  "source_issue": "canonical public-style URI",
  "objective": "human-readable outcome",
  "repository": {"url": "...", "ref": "..."},
  "dependencies": ["task IDs"],
  "workspace": {"kind": "git-worktree"},
  "capabilities": ["filesystem:write", "git:commit", "network:none"],
  "approval_policy": "explicit-for-destructive-or-external",
  "acceptance_checks": ["command or named check"],
  "budget": {"tokens": null, "wall_time_seconds": 3600},
  "artifacts": [],
  "state": "queued"
}
```

Keep lifecycle states deliberately small: `queued → claimed → running → needs_input|blocked|failed|completed → accepted`. Record append-only events; derive dashboards from those events instead of letting every harness mutate an opaque status object.

### 3. Terminal project cockpit

[NTM](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm) is the closest open component to the complete cockpit described here. It uses tmux as the execution substrate and adds:

- Named mixed-agent sessions
- Dispatch, interruption and follow-up operations
- Beads graph triage and assignment
- Agent messaging and file reservations
- Safety policies and approvals
- Worktree support
- Checkpoints, timelines and audit records
- JSON “robot” interfaces plus REST, SSE, WebSocket and OpenAPI surfaces

That last point makes NTM more reusable than a visually attractive TUI with no control API.

Smaller alternatives worth evaluating:

- [agent-deck](https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck): polished tmux-backed TUI for organizing Claude, Codex, Gemini and OpenCode sessions.
- [workmux](https://github.com/raine/workmux): focused mapping of one task to one Git worktree and tmux window.
- [Flowmux](https://github.com/grouzen/flowmux): keyboard-first dashboard over real agent CLIs, projects and worktrees.
- [agtx](https://github.com/fynnfluegge/agtx): Kanban/spec-driven orchestration with isolated worktrees.
- [OpenSwarm](https://github.com/matars/OpenSwarm): niche graph-oriented TUI for parallel agents across worktrees.
- [muxel](https://github.com/muxel-dev/muxel): broader terminal/worktree/agent environment; useful if you want more of the terminal itself replaced.

### Suggested starting stack

I would begin with:

1. OpenProject—or the company’s existing GitHub/GitLab—as canonical.
2. A thin Go or TypeScript synchronizer producing normalized task and edge events.
3. Beads/Dolt as the agent execution projection.
4. AGENTS.md plus versioned JSON Schemas stored in each repository.
5. MCP servers for issue, source-control and CI operations.
6. NTM/tmux for the operator cockpit, with one Git worktree per mutable task.
7. OpenTelemetry into an open backend such as [Grafana Tempo](https://github.com/grafana/tempo) for audit and performance analysis.

The main architectural rule is separation: the issue tracker records company intent, the execution graph records agent-ready work, the contracts define portable behavior, and the cockpit observes and controls processes. This prevents whichever terminal orchestrator is fashionable this quarter from becoming your permanent company data model.

results.stdout:
Kevin Rajan frames code as an equalizer because software—and increasingly LLMs—democratizes knowledge and engineering. It lets more people turn ideas into working systems, allowing “competence [to compound] without gatekeepers.”

By “automating humanitarian causes,” he means applying autonomous systems to foundational public needs such as:

- Health
- Infrastructure
- Open systems that give people greater agency

His broader thesis is that civilization advances when important actions become dependable enough to happen without continual human attention. Automation should therefore extend human capacity—not merely optimize convenience—producing greater abundance and quality of life.

In short: **code distributes capability; humanitarian automation turns that capability into durable agency and essential services.**

Source: Kevin Rajan’s canonical [Boplog build log](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/) and its [automation systems hub](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/automation.html).

These describe public work only and do not establish any private roadmap or deployment.\n", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:46: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:54: "stdout": "tmux-agent-fleet is kvnloo’s open-source tmux plugin for quickly finding, monitoring, and switching between coding-agent panes.\n\nIt turns `prefix + f` into a searchable `fzf` command palette that:\n\n- Discovers active agents directly from tmux process metadata—no daemon or agent hooks.\n- Supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Oh My Pi, Pi, Fable, ordinary shells, and optional Agent Deck sessions.\n- Shows a live pane preview and jumps to the selected pane.\n- Avoids injecting commands, renaming sessions, managing worktrees, or sending telemetry.\n- Uses pywal colors when available, with built-in fallback styling.\n\nIt is a switcher and monitor, not an agent orchestrator. Because it is harness-neutral and hook-free, its activity indicator reflects pane activity rather than semantic states such as “waiting for permission.”\n\nPublic build-log fields classify it as:\n\n- Type: public, Shell\n- Category: dev\n- Company: zer0\n- Kind: product\n- Product: agent tooling\n- Public record date: July 14, 2026\n- License: MIT\n\nSources:\n- Canonical build log: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/\n- Repository: https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet\n", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:56: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:66: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:76: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:84: "stdout": "Kevin Rajan’s canonical [boplog build log](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/) marks six projects as featured:\n\n1. [AudioEngine](https://github.com/kvnloo/AudioEngine) — A 2017 iOS project featuring a real-time noise meter and 14-band dual-channel equalizer.\n2. [ace](https://github.com/kvnloo/ace) — A demo site and digital twin of an autonomous, multi-floor racket-sports facility.\n4. [evolve](https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve) — An agent-swarm and multi-agent orchestration toolkit built around Claude Code agents, documentation, and examples.\n5. His public work focuses on using AI and code to increase individual agency\u2014particularly through autonomous-development systems, agent tooling, health technology, and simulations.\n\nPublicly, he is known for:\n\n- AI-agent infrastructure and autonomous development\n - `tmux-agent-fleet`: a zero-daemon command palette for coordinating coding agents across tmux panes.\n - `evolve`: a multi-agent orchestration toolkit built around Claude Code agents.\n - Tools for agent monitoring, verification harnesses, and evidence-based \u201cdone\u201d states.\n\n- `zerOS`\n - A stealth company-operating-system track under zer0.\n - Public components include issue-graph and scheduling infrastructure (`_pm`), a terminal cockpit, agent-harness contracts, and voice adapters.\n - The public description intentionally provides limited product detail.\n\n- Digital twins and interactive simulations\n - `ace`: a digital twin of an autonomous, multi-floor racket-sports facility.\n - Other public experiments include Three.js environments, generative art, 3D scene tooling, and infotainment-interface prototypes.\n\n- Health and human-performance technology\n - Health and peak performance are recurring themes in his stated mission and one of zer0\u2019s public product tracks.\n\n- Earlier mobile and audio engineering\n - `AudioEngine`, dating to 2017, includes an iOS real-time noise meter and a 14-band dual-channel equalizer.\n\nHis canonical public build log currently catalogs 52 repositories from 2017\u20132026 where he authored at least one commit: 25 products, 18 experiments, and 9 professional projects. It deliberately excludes private repositories and forks he merely bookmarked, so it should be understood as a verified public-build archive\u2014not a complete r\u00e9sum\u00e9 or account of private work.\n\nSources:\n\n- Canonical build log and biography: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/\n- Machine-readable site guide: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/llms.txt\n- Public project manifest: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/data/manifest.json\n- GitHub profile: https://github.com/kvnloo\n- X: https://x.com/_kvnloo\n\nIn one sentence: Kevin Rajan is publicly known as an AI-focused builder creating agent orchestration tools, autonomous-development infrastructure, company-OS components, simulations, and human-performance technology under the zer0 umbrella.\n", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T09-18-27-merged/raw.json:97: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T09-18-27-merged/raw.json:107: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T09-18-27-merged/raw.json:117: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T09-18-27-merged/raw.json:127: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T09-18-27-merged/raw.json:137: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T09-18-27-merged/raw.json:145: "stdout": "Kevin Rajan\u2019s canonical [boplog build log](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/) marks six projects as featured:\n\n1. The archive covers public GitHub repositories where `kvnloo` authored commits; it excludes private work and untouched bookmark-only forks.\n", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T09-18-27-merged/raw.json:147: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T09-18-27-merged/raw.json:157: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T09-18-27-merged/raw.json:167: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T09-18-27-merged/raw.json:175: "stdout": "Evolve is Kevin Rajan\u2019s public autonomous AI development and multi-agent orchestration project.\n\nIt combines several agent-development tools into one systematic workflow:\n\n- Claude Flow and SPARC for specification, architecture, TDD, and coordinated execution\n- CCPM for PRDs, issue decomposition, GitHub synchronization, and worktrees\n- SuperClaude for behavioral and research modes\n- Claude Squad for parallel agent sessions\n- Continuous Claude for iterative development and PR automation\n- Claude Code as the main execution engine\n\nIts central concept is C(RAID): Research \u2192 Analysis \u2192 Integration \u2192 Deployment \u2192 feedback, an AI-oriented alternative to a conventional code-first CI/CD cycle.\n\nThe canonical build-log record classifies Evolve as:\n\n- Company umbrella: zer0\n- Kind: product\n- Product: evolve\n- Blueprint track: 3\n- Category: dev\n- Primary language: Shell\n- Public-record date: December 2, 2025\n- License: MIT\n- Repository: https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve\n- Documentation: https://kvnloo.github.io/evolve/\n\nIn short, Evolve is intended as an end-to-end framework for autonomous software development in which specialized AI agents research, plan, implement, test, review, and manage delivery across isolated sessions.\n\nSources: [canonical boplog record](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/), [public Evolve documentation](https://kvnloo.github.io/evolve/), and [GitHub repository](https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve). These describe public work only and do not establish any private roadmap or deployment.\n", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T09-18-27-merged/raw.json:177: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T09-18-27-merged/raw.json:185: "stdout": "tmux-agent-fleet is kvnloo\u2019s open-source tmux plugin for quickly finding, monitoring, and switching between coding-agent panes.\n\nIt turns `prefix + f` into a searchable `fzf` command palette that:\n\n- Discovers active agents directly from tmux process metadata\u2014no daemon or agent hooks.\n- Supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Oh My Pi, Pi, Fable, ordinary shells, and optional Agent Deck sessions.\n- Shows a live pane preview and jumps to the selected pane.\n- Avoids injecting commands, renaming sessions, managing worktrees, or sending telemetry.\n- Uses pywal colors when available, with built-in fallback styling.\n\nIt is a switcher and monitor, not an agent orchestrator. results.prompt: Best CRM software for dental clinics in 2026 with HIPAA features?
results.stdout:
As of July 2026, my strongest default recommendation for a typical U.S. dental clinic is **RevenueWell**. For a modern front-office/patient-experience layer, choose **NexHealth**. Larger groups needing true lead management should consider **LeadSquared**, while clinics replacing their entire practice-management system should evaluate **CareStack** or **tab32**.

| Product | Best for | Relevant HIPAA/security evidence | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| [RevenueWell](https://www.revenuewell.com/hipaa-compliance) | Best overall for independent dental practices | Dental-specific communications and recall; encrypted PMS data transfer; publishes [HIPAA Business Associate Terms](https://assets-global.website-files.com/61f084e913f6528e6d44ef9d/626ad3505d77e19bb1ed490d_RW_HIPAA-Business-Associate-Terms.pdf) | More patient engagement/marketing than sophisticated sales CRM |
| [NexHealth](https://www.nexhealth.com/) | Best patient experience and front-office automation | Booking, forms, messaging, recalls, payments, verification and PMS synchronization; its [Trust Center](https://security.nexhealth.com/) lists HIPAA, SOC 2, MFA, audit logging and penetration testing | Confirm BAA availability, covered modules and exact PMS write-back behavior in your contract |
| [Weave](https://www.getweave.com/security/) | Best phone-and-text-centered workflow | Dental communications, phones and payments; vendor documents HIPAA-supporting features, penetration testing, backups and resilient GCP infrastructure | Less capable for formal lead pipelines and multi-stage case acceptance |
| [Dental Intelligence / Modento](https://www.dentalintel.com/terms/baa) | Best analytics, scheduling and patient engagement around an existing PMS | Public BAA explicitly includes Dental Intelligence, LocalMed and Modento | Ordinary email and SMS should not contain sensitive PHI; Dental Intelligence says its protected in-app messaging is the compliant channel |
| [LeadSquared Dental CRM](https://www.leadsquared.com/us/healthcare/crm-for-dental-practices/) | Best true CRM for DSOs and high-value treatment leads | BAA, encryption at rest/in transit, RBAC and audit trails; integrations listed for Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental, Curve and Carestream | Heavier implementation and likely excessive for a small general practice |
| [CareStack](https://carestack.com/dental-software/features/hipaa-compliant) | Best all-in-one PMS replacement for growing groups | Identifies itself as a HIPAA business associate; audit trail, job-based permissions, encrypted communications and backups; also reports SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001:2022 | This is a full dental operating platform, not merely a CRM add-on |
| [tab32](https://tab32.com/platform/) | Best cloud PMS for DSOs and data/analytics access | Vendor reports HIPAA support, SOC 2 Type II, encryption at rest/in transit, RBAC, audit trails and enterprise SSO | Migration is substantially larger than installing a CRM alongside your existing PMS |

My practical shortlist:

- **One-to-five locations, keeping Dentrix/Eaglesoft/Open Dental:** demo RevenueWell, NexHealth and Weave.
- **Growth-heavy implant, cosmetic or orthodontic clinic:** LeadSquared, especially if lead attribution and treatment-conversion pipelines matter.
- **Multi-location DSO:** LeadSquared over the existing PMS, or CareStack/tab32 if consolidating the entire technology stack.
- **Analytics and reactivation are the priority:** Dental Intelligence/Modento.

Open-source options exist, but none is a turnkey dental CRM I would place ahead of those products:

- [SuiteCRM](https://github.com/SuiteCRM/SuiteCRM) is a mature, customizable open-source CRM. It can be self-hosted, but the software itself does **not** make the resulting deployment HIPAA compliant; you own infrastructure, audit logging, backups, access control, incident response and every relevant BAA.
- [OpenEMR](https://github.com/openemr/openemr) provides open-source EHR, scheduling and billing, but is medical rather than dental-specific and needs expert security administration.
- [SiftDental Community](https://github.com/fortunatus-collab/siftdental-community) and [open-dentist](https://github.com/clawnify/open-dentist) are interesting niche dental projects, but I would treat them as development foundations—not production HIPAA solutions—until independently assessed.

Before signing, require written answers covering:

1. A signed BAA **before any PHI enters the system**, including applicable subcontractors.
2. MFA, role-based access, immutable audit history and rapid user deprovisioning.
3. Encryption in transit and at rest, documented backups, disaster recovery and breach notification.
4. Exactly which email, SMS, AI transcription and call-recording workflows may carry PHI.
5. A live test of your exact PMS integration—especially two-way scheduling, form write-back, duplicate handling and ledger/payment synchronization.
6. Data export and deletion terms when the contract ends.

This is important because HHS does not certify CRM products as “HIPAA compliant.” HHS says a cloud provider handling ePHI generally requires a HIPAA-compliant BAA, while the clinic must still conduct its own risk analysis and implement appropriate controls. See the official [HHS cloud-computing guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html) and [sample BAA provisions](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/covered-entities/sample-business-associate-agreement-provisions/index.html).

## Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta

Ready in about 25 minutes; serves 2 generously.

### Ingredients

- 8 oz (225 g) pasta
- 8 oz (225 g) mushrooms, sliced
- 3 packed cups baby spinach
- 2 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- ½ cup heavy cream, crème fraîche, or cream cheese
- ⅓ cup grated Parmesan
- ½ tsp red-pepper flakes, optional
- Salt and black pepper
- Optional: lemon zest or a squeeze of lemon

### Method

1. Boil the pasta in salted water. Before draining, reserve ½ cup pasta water.
2. Meanwhile, heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add the mushrooms, spread them out, and leave them undisturbed for 2–3 minutes. Season and cook until browned, another 4–5 minutes.
3. Add the garlic and pepper flakes; cook for 30 seconds.
4. Reduce the heat. Stir in the cream and Parmesan, followed by the spinach.
5. Add the drained pasta and a splash of pasta water. Toss until the spinach wilts and the sauce becomes glossy, adding more water as needed.
6. Finish with black pepper and lemon.

The key is giving the mushrooms space and time to brown before adding anything wet. This is adapted into a pantry-friendly format from [Good Food’s 25-minute creamy mushroom and spinach pasta](https://www.bbcgoodfood.com/recipes/creamy-mushroom-spinach-pasta).

For extra protein, add white beans, shredded chicken, or browned Italian sausage.

# Agent Reach — 互联网能力路由器

15 平台、多后端。**本 skill 存在时必须用它访问这些平台，不要自己发明方案。**

1. **动手前先体检**：多后端/登录态平台（小红书/Reddit/B站/Twitter/Facebook/Instagram）先跑
   `agent-reach doctor --json`，按各平台 `active_backend` 字段选命令组。

5. **替用户盯版本**：完成一次较大的调研/多平台任务后，顺手跑
   `agent-reach check-update`（很快，一个 API 调用）。有新版就在收尾汇报里附一句：

```bash

# 通用网页阅读
curl -s "https://r.jina.ai/URL"

# YouTube 字幕（注意：B站不要用 yt-dlp，见 video.md）
```
